blocks.text: “He was almost well again, but Mr. Hawkins’s death has upset him very much.” He interrupted me:—
“Oh, yes, I know, I know. I have read your last two letters.” I went on:—
“I suppose this upset him. When we were in town last Thursday, he had a kind of shock.”
“A shock, and after brain fever so soon! That was not good. What kind of a shock was it?”

“He thought he saw someone who made him remember something terrible. It was the thing that led to his brain fever.” And at this point everything suddenly seemed too much for me. It all came over me in a rush. I felt pity for Jonathan. I thought of the horror he had lived through, and the whole fearful mystery of his diary. I felt the fear that has hung over me ever since. All of this came at once, in a wild confusion. I suppose I was hysterical, because I threw myself on my knees. I held up my hands to him and begged him to make my husband well again. He took my hands and raised me up. He made me sit on the sofa, and he sat beside me. He held my hand in his, and he spoke to me with, oh, such endless sweetness:—

“My life is empty and lonely. It is so full of work that I have not had much time for friendships. But my friend John Seward called me to come here. Since then I have known so many good people, and I have seen such noble goodness. Because of this, I feel the loneliness of my life more than ever. And this feeling has grown stronger as I have grown older. So believe me: I come here full of respect for you. And you have given me hope. It is not hope about the thing I am searching for. It is hope that there are still good women left to make life happy. These are good women whose lives and whose truths may be a good lesson for the children who will be born in the future. I am glad, glad, that I can be of some use to you here. If your husband suffers, his suffering is the kind I have studied and know from experience. I promise you that I will gladly do all I can for him. I will do all I can to make his life strong and manly, and to make your life a happy one. Now you must eat. You are too tired and upset, and perhaps you worry too much. Husband Jonathan would not like to see you so pale. And what he does not like to see in the one he loves is not good for him. So for his sake you must eat and smile. You have told me all about Lucy, so now we shall not speak of it, in case it upsets you. I shall stay in Exeter tonight. I want to think a lot about what you have told me. When I have thought about it, I will ask you questions, if I may. And then you will also tell me about husband Jonathan’s trouble, as far as you can. But not yet. You must eat now. Afterwards you shall tell me everything.”
After lunch, when we went back to the drawing-room, he said to me:—

“And now tell me all about him.” Now I had to speak to this great and learned man. I began to fear that he would think I was a weak fool, and that Jonathan was a madman. That journal is all so strange! So I stopped, unsure whether to go on. But he was so sweet and kind. He had promised to help, and I trusted him. So I said:—

“Dr. Van Helsing, what I have to tell you is so strange that you must not laugh at me or at my husband. Since yesterday I have been in a kind of fever of doubt. You must be kind to me. Please do not think I am foolish because I have even half believed some very strange things.” He calmed my fears, both by the way he behaved and by his words, when he said:—

“Oh, my dear, if you only knew how strange the matter is that brings me here! Then it is you who would laugh. I have learned never to think little of anyone’s belief, however strange it is. I have tried to keep an open mind. It is not the ordinary things of life that could close my mind. It is the strange things, the extraordinary things, the things that make a person wonder if they are mad or sane.”
